# Slidr design quality instruction

When creating or changing templates, ready-made slide designs, invitations, marketing slides, video thumbnails, or examples in Elements:

- Produce work that looks professionally art directed and publication ready. A flat background, a heading, and a few basic shapes are a wireframe. Give every design a clear concept, relevant imagery or crafted illustration, refined typography, purposeful detail, and a strong focal point.
- Make each example visually distinct for its purpose. Changing only colors or swapping a title does not count as a different design.
- When a visual reference is supplied, compare its subject scale, typography, contrast, decorative density, layering and sense of movement with the rendered result. Match the level of craft; do not add arbitrary ornaments that cross text, faces or key product details.
- Use original, meaningful sample text. Do not ship placeholder text, dummy image frames, lorem ipsum, or stale event dates. Keep text and useful framing elements editable. Bundle image assets with the presentation so the design survives saving and works offline.
- In a template, most of what a slide shows is the slide's own, to select, move, restyle and delete: a layout gives its drawings to its slides as objects (`withObjects` in `packages/templates/src/builtin/kit.ts`, ADR-094). Only what frames every slide stays in the layout: the foot with the logo and the slide's number, and a ground or border that covers the slide. Draw a scene as its parts, each in a box of its own, not as one drawing the size of the slide, and keep drawings clear of the foot. `packages/templates/src/authoring/check.ts` fails a template that keeps its drawings.
- A template's text slide gives the text the room: the title across the top, and under it a card or panel in the template's own form from margin to margin, down to 24–32px above the foot, with the body inside it about 1600px wide and set from the top (never centred in its box). The drawing shrinks to a small accent in the margin or on a corner of the card, clear of the text. Its sample, in every language, is a lead of two lines and four points of one line each, numbered, each opening with a few words in bold. `check.ts` checks the layout and the sample's shape; the renders show the lines.
- Write every design in Hebrew and English, and in another language only when the request names it (the languages are listed in `packages/model/src/languages.ts`; the event frames of Elements stay in Hebrew and English). Render every design at full slide size and thumbnail size in each of its languages. Inspect the actual rendered pixels. Fix text overflow, awkward wraps, clipping, weak contrast, poor photo crops, uneven alignment, and RTL mistakes, then render again.
- Set each language's text in a family of the library that has its letters (`fonts/catalog.json` in the media library: a family's `scripts`). Keep the design's character in every language: where the English text (for Arabic, the Hebrew text it mirrors) is set in a family without another language's letters, that language sets the same text in the family's `counterparts` entry for its script, the closest family in character (Playfair Display → Frank Ruhl Libre in Hebrew, Amiri in Arabic, Noto Serif Devanagari in Hindi, Noto Serif JP in Japanese), at the same weight or the nearest one the counterpart has. Never set every text of a language in one family just because it has the letters, and never leave a language to the system's fonts. `node apps/desktop/scripts/design-fonts.mjs` applies this to the designs of the library, and `designs.test.ts` checks it.
- Do not call the work done merely because schema validation or automated tests pass. Include a visual review of every design and correct what that review reveals.
